strings.name: Irene Khan
strings.role: Permanent Representative of Bangladesh to the United Nations and human rights advocate
strings.summary: Irene Khan is a Bangladeshi human rights advocate and diplomat who led Amnesty International and the International Development Law Organization, and served as UN Special Rapporteur on freedom of expression from 2020 to 2026. Her work spans refugees, women’s rights, poverty and the rule of law. In August 2026 she became Bangladesh’s permanent representative to the UN.
strings.coverageNote: Sources checked through 18 November 2026. The UN’s 4 November protocol list confirms her current office, and the mission has an indexed General Assembly statement dated 5 November. Her Special Rapporteur tenure ended in July; older biographies describing that mandate as current are not carried forward.
strings.influence.rationale: Former leader of Amnesty International and UN Special Rapporteur on freedom of expression, promoting international human rights protection and the right to public expression.
strings.facts.f1.label: Birth and legal education
strings.facts.f1.value: Born in Dhaka in 1956, then in East Pakistan and now Bangladesh. She went to Northern Ireland for school as a teenager, then studied law at the University of Manchester and Harvard Law School, focusing on public international law and human rights.
strings.facts.f2.label: Poverty and rights
strings.facts.f2.value: Published The Unheard Truth: Poverty and Human Rights in 2009, connecting poverty with human rights. Her work in civil society, international institutions and diplomacy encompasses gender equality, expression, legal protection and development.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Women’s rights and public expression
strings.highlights.h1.text: As Amnesty’s leader she promoted its global campaign against violence toward women, launched in 2004. As Special Rapporteur she addressed women’s expression, disinformation, exiled journalists and Big Tech. That independent expert mandate differs from her later diplomatic responsibilities representing Bangladesh’s government.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Departure payments and institutional accountability
strings.highlights.h2.text: Amnesty’s departure payments drew controversy in 2011. Its Executive Committee disclosed that £533,103 paid to Khan in the financial year ending March 2010 included salary and earlier arrears, with £191,697 related to termination. After an independent review, Amnesty acknowledged governance and management failings behind excessive payments. This was not an individual criminal conviction.
strings.timeline.t1.title: Becomes Bangladesh’s permanent representative to the UN
strings.timeline.t1.text: Presented credentials to UN Secretary-General António Guterres in New York, formally beginning her tenure. The UN protocol list confirms the date. Her appointment reported in July and her formal assumption of duties in August are separate milestones.
strings.timeline.t2.title: Ends tenure as freedom of expression rapporteur
strings.timeline.t2.text: Completed the six-year tenure begun in 2020. ARTICLE 19 marked the occasion with a review of her work on gender, information environments and journalists’ protection. Ending the mandate did not mean retiring from human rights or public affairs.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Begins work as UN Special Rapporteur
strings.timeline.t3.text: Took office as Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of the right to freedom of opinion and expression, the first woman in the role. She undertook independent expert work through reports, communications with governments and country visits; her views were not court judgments.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Takes office as IDLO Director-General
strings.timeline.t4.text: Became the first woman to lead IDLO. Member Parties elected her on 17 November 2011, and she formally began work on New Year’s Day 2012. Her tenure lasted until the end of 2019, with successor Jan Beagle taking office on 1 January 2020.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Leaves Amnesty International’s leadership
strings.timeline.t5.text: Departed by agreement after two terms. The Executive Committee later explained its decision to change leadership and negotiate the end of her employment. Her departure, payments in the 2010 financial year and the public controversy in 2011 were distinct stages.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Receives the Sydney Peace Prize
strings.timeline.t6.text: The citation recognized her leadership for universal human rights and her work making violence against women a major injustice to confront through peace campaigning. The award was the Sydney Peace Prize, not the Nobel Peace Prize.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Leads Amnesty International
strings.timeline.t7.text: Became its seventh Secretary General and the first woman, Asian and Muslim to hold that office. She expanded work on economic, social and cultural rights and led international advocacy in the aftermath of the September 11 attacks.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Joins UNHCR
strings.timeline.t8.text: Began roughly 21 years of refugee-protection work at headquarters and in field operations. She became head of mission in India in 1995, led the team in what was then Macedonia during the 1999 Kosovo crisis, and subsequently became Deputy Director of International Protection.
